paragraphs: It is not a new observation that the people of any country, if they are intelligent and well-informed as the Americans are, seldom adopt an erroneous opinion about their interests and hold to it steadily for many years. That consideration naturally creates great respect for the opinion that the people of America have so long and so uniformly held, that it is important for them to remain firmly united under one federal government, given enough powers for all general and national purposes.
The more attentively I consider and investigate the reasons that appear to have given birth to this opinion, the more I am convinced that they are compelling and conclusive.

Among the many objects to which a wise and free people must direct their attention, providing for their SAFETY seems to come first. The SAFETY of the people doubtless relates to a great variety of circumstances and considerations, and so allows great latitude to those who wish to define it precisely and comprehensively.

At present I mean to consider it only as it concerns security for the preservation of peace and tranquillity, both against dangers from FOREIGN ARMS AND INFLUENCE and against dangers of the LIKE KIND arising from domestic causes. Since the former comes first in order, it is proper that it be discussed first. Let us therefore proceed to examine whether the people are not right in their opinion that a cordial Union, under an effective national government, gives them the best security that can be devised against HOSTILITIES from abroad.

The number of wars that have happened or will happen in the world will always be found proportionate to the number and weight of the causes, whether REAL or PRETENDED, that PROVOKE or INVITE them. If this remark is just, it becomes useful to inquire whether UNITED AMERICA is likely to give as many JUST causes of war as DISUNITED America. For if it should turn out that United America will probably give the fewest, it will follow that, in this respect, the Union does the most to preserve the people in a state of peace with other nations.

The JUST causes of war, for the most part, arise either from violations of treaties or from direct violence. America has already formed treaties with no fewer than six foreign nations, and all of them except Prussia are maritime powers and therefore able to annoy and injure us. She also has extensive commerce with Portugal, Spain, and Britain, and with the latter two she has, in addition, the circumstance of neighborhood to attend to.

It is of high importance to the peace of America that she observe the laws of nations toward all these powers, and it appears evident to me that this will be done more perfectly and punctually by one national government than it could be by thirteen separate States or by three or four distinct confederacies.

The reason is, first, that once an effective national government is established, the best men in the country will not only consent to serve but will generally be the ones appointed to run it. Town or county influence, or other narrow influence, may place men in State assemblies, senates, courts of justice, or executive departments. But a wider and more extensive reputation for talents and other qualifications will be necessary to recommend men to offices under the national government, especially as it will have the widest field to choose from and will never experience the shortage of suitable persons that is not uncommon in some of the States. It will therefore follow that the administration, the political counsels, and the judicial decisions of the national government will be wiser, more systematic, and more judicious than those of the individual States, and consequently more satisfactory to other nations as well as more SAFE for us.

The reason is, second, that under the national government, treaties and the articles of treaties, as well as the laws of nations, will always be interpreted in one sense and carried out in the same manner. Rulings on the same points and questions in thirteen States, or in three or four confederacies, will not always agree or be consistent. This is so both because of the variety of independent courts and judges appointed by different and independent governments, and because of the different local laws and interests that may affect and influence them. The wisdom of the convention in committing such questions to the jurisdiction and judgment of courts appointed by, and responsible only to, one national government cannot be too highly praised.

The reason is, third, that the prospect of present loss or advantage may often tempt the governing party in one or two States to depart from good faith and justice. But those temptations do not reach the other States, and so have little or no influence on the national government. The temptation will therefore be fruitless, and good faith and justice will be preserved. The case of the treaty of peace with Britain adds great weight to this reasoning.

The reason is, fourth, that even if the governing party in a State were disposed to resist such temptations, they may, and commonly do, result from circumstances peculiar to the State, and may affect a great number of its inhabitants. The governing party may then not always be able, even if willing, to prevent the injustice intended or to punish those who commit it. But the national government, not being affected by those local circumstances, will neither be induced to commit the wrong itself nor lack the power or the will to prevent or punish its commission by others.

So far, therefore, as violations of treaties and of the laws of nations, whether intended or accidental, give JUST causes of war, they are less to be feared under one general government than under several lesser ones, and in that respect the former does most to favor the SAFETY of the people.

As to those just causes of war that arise from direct and unlawful violence, it seems equally clear to me that one good national government gives far more security against dangers of that sort than can be had from any other source.

The reason is that such violence is more frequently caused by the passions and interests of a part than of the whole, of one or two States than of the Union. Not a single Indian war has yet been caused by aggressions of the present federal government, feeble as it is. But there are several instances of Indian hostilities provoked by the improper conduct of individual States which, being either unable or unwilling to restrain or punish offenses, have given occasion for the slaughter of many innocent inhabitants.

The nearness of Spanish and British territories, which border on some States and not on others, naturally confines the causes of quarrel more directly to the States along the border. The bordering States, if any, will be those that, under the impulse of sudden irritation and a quick sense of apparent interest or injury, are most likely to provoke war with these nations by direct violence. Nothing can so effectively prevent that danger as a national government, whose wisdom and prudence will not be reduced by the passions that move the parties immediately concerned.

But the national government will not only give fewer just causes of war; it will also be more in its power to accommodate and settle them peacefully. It will be more temperate and cool, and in that respect, as in others, will be better able to act with deliberation than the offending State. The pride of states, like that of men, naturally disposes them to justify all their actions and stands in the way of their acknowledging, correcting, or repairing their errors and offenses. The national government, in such cases, will not be affected by this pride, but will proceed with moderation and fairness to consider and decide on the means best suited to extricate them from the difficulties that threaten them.

Besides, it is well known that acknowledgments, explanations, and compensations are often accepted as satisfactory from a strong united nation that would be rejected as unsatisfactory if offered by a State or confederacy of little consideration or power.

In the year 1685, the state of Genoa, having offended Louis XIV, tried to appease him. He demanded that they send their Doge, or chief executive, accompanied by four of their senators, to FRANCE, to ask his pardon and receive his terms. They were obliged to submit to it for the sake of peace. Would he, on any occasion, have either demanded or received the like humiliation from Spain, or Britain, or any other POWERFUL nation?
